subtopic_detail: recognising drug induced inner restlessness that has been misread as worsening agitation
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the ward about a 46 year old man with schizophrenia whose antipsychotic was changed to aripiprazole three weeks ago. The nursing staff have documented increasing agitation and have given two doses of an oral as needed antipsychotic over the past two days, after each of which they record that he became more unsettled rather than less.

He tells you that he cannot describe it properly but that he feels a dreadful restlessness inside, that he cannot stay in a chair and has to keep moving, and that it is there from the moment he wakes until he falls asleep. He paces the corridor and rocks from foot to foot while standing talking to you. He says his psychotic symptoms have actually improved and denies feeling frightened or angry with anyone.

data_table.Examination: Constant shifting of weight while standing, inability to remain seated for more than a minute, no tremor, no cogwheel rigidity, no orofacial dyskinesia, mental state examination shows settled thought content with improved delusional conviction
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 140 micrograms/L (30 to 300), full blood count within normal limits, creatine kinase within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce the antipsychotic dose and commence propranolol for the symptom
options.rationale: Subjective inner restlessness with observable motor restlessness beginning within weeks of an antipsychotic change is drug induced akathisia, and dose reduction addresses the cause while a lipophilic beta blocker is the best supported symptomatic treatment. Recognising it matters because akathisia is associated with increased suicide risk and with treatment discontinuation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Increase the antipsychotic dose to settle what appears to be agitation
options.rationale: This is the error the ward has already made twice, and the record that he worsened after each as needed dose is the clue. Treating akathisia as psychotic agitation escalates the very drug causing it and produces a cycle of increasing dose and increasing distress. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence benztropine and review the response over the next few days
options.rationale: Anticholinergic agents are effective for drug induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia but perform poorly for akathisia, which is the extrapyramidal syndrome they do not treat. He has neither tremor nor cogwheel rigidity to suggest parkinsonism. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence a dopamine agonist taken in the evening before he goes to bed
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists treat restless legs syndrome, in which the urge is localised to the legs, is worst in the evening and at rest, and is relieved by movement. His restlessness is generalised and constant throughout the day, his ferritin is not low, and a dopamine agonist risks aggravating psychosis. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

options.text: Commence oral iron replacement and recheck the ferritin in three months
options.rationale: Iron deficiency drives restless legs syndrome and replacement is indicated when ferritin falls below about 75 micrograms/L. His ferritin is well above that threshold, so there is no deficiency to correct. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association)

explanation.summary: Akathisia is a subjective sense of inner restlessness accompanied by an inability to remain still, and it is among the most distressing adverse effects of antipsychotic medication. It is most common in the first weeks after starting or increasing a drug, and aripiprazole is notable for causing it despite otherwise favourable extrapyramidal tolerability. The central clinical danger is misattribution: the outward picture of a pacing, unsettled patient is easily recorded as agitation or as worsening psychosis, which leads to dose escalation or additional as needed antipsychotic and a worsening cycle, and a documented deterioration after each as needed dose is the pattern that should prompt reconsideration. Restless legs syndrome is the main differential and is separated by the localisation of the urge to the legs, the circadian worsening in the evening and at rest, relief with movement, and an association with low ferritin. Management is reduction of the causative dose or a switch to an agent with lower liability, with propranolol as the best supported symptomatic treatment and benzodiazepines or mirtazapine as alternatives, while anticholinergics are ineffective.
key_points: Akathisia combines subjective inner restlessness with observable motor restlessness
It appears within weeks of starting or increasing an antipsychotic
Misreading it as agitation leads to dose escalation and a worsening cycle
Anticholinergics treat parkinsonism and dystonia but not akathisia
Restless legs is localised to the legs, worse at rest in the evening, and linked to low ferritin
explanation.pearls: A patient who becomes more unsettled after each as needed dose of antipsychotic has akathisia rather than agitation, and propranolol 10 to 20 mg three times daily alongside dose reduction is the response, not another dose of the drug causing it.

subtopic_detail: acting on a markedly prolonged QT interval with correctable electrolyte abnormalities and additive drug effects
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on an inpatient unit reviewing a 52 year old woman with schizoaffective disorder. She has been taking citalopram 40 mg daily and haloperidol, and over the past week she has had repeated vomiting attributed to a gastrointestinal illness and has eaten very little.

This morning she felt light headed on standing and the nursing staff obtained an electrocardiogram. She has no chest pain and no palpitations, has never had a syncopal episode, and has no known cardiac disease. A previous electrocardiogram taken on admission six weeks ago was reported as normal. Her results are available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 58, blood pressure 106/68, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, no murmur, heart sounds dual, chest clear, no peripheral oedema, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.05), corrected calcium within normal limits, creatinine mildly raised, thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus bradycardia at 58 beats per minute with a corrected QT interval of 510 milliseconds, no ischaemic changes, compared with 430 milliseconds six weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue both medications and repeat the electrocardiogram in a week
options.rationale: An interval above 500 milliseconds with ongoing electrolyte depletion and bradycardia represents a present risk of a malignant arrhythmia rather than a trend to observe. A week of unchanged treatment leaves every contributing factor in place. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Replace potassium and magnesium with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia are the fastest reversible contributors to the prolonged interval and both must be corrected promptly, with magnesium replaced even when the level is only modestly low because it stabilises the myocardium. Continuous monitoring is required at this interval because the risk of torsades de pointes rises steeply beyond 500 milliseconds. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Cease the antipsychotic alone and continue the antidepressant unchanged
options.rationale: Both drugs prolong the interval and their effects are additive, and citalopram is specifically dose dependent in this respect with 40 mg exceeding the maximum recommended dose for patients over 60 and carrying a regulatory warning at any age. Stopping only one leaves a substantial pharmacological contribution untreated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium only if torsades de pointes actually occurs
options.rationale: Magnesium is certainly the treatment once the arrhythmia has begun, which is why this option feels familiar, but withholding it until then forgoes the opportunity to prevent an event that can be fatal on first occurrence. Prophylactic correction of a documented deficiency is standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Switch immediately to a different antipsychotic at an equivalent dose
options.rationale: A switch to a lower risk agent will form part of the plan, but choosing and titrating a new antipsychotic is a decision for the coming days rather than the immediate response. It does nothing about the electrolytes or the bradycardia, which are the acute drivers. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Drug induced QT prolongation results from blockade of the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current, and risk accumulates additively across contributing factors rather than resting on any single one. The relevant factors here are two QT prolonging drugs taken together, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia and female sex, which independently confers a longer baseline interval. Absolute thresholds matter for action: an interval above 500 milliseconds, or an increase of more than 60 milliseconds from baseline, marks a substantially increased risk of torsades de pointes, and this patient meets both criteria. Citalopram carries a specific dose dependent warning, with maximum recommended doses of 40 mg in adults and 20 mg in those over 60 or with hepatic impairment. Immediate management corrects the reversible physiological contributors, which means replacing potassium to the upper half of the reference range and giving magnesium even when only mildly low, with continuous monitoring, while rationalisation of the psychotropic regimen follows once the acute risk is controlled.
key_points: Risk accumulates additively across drugs, electrolytes, bradycardia and sex
An interval above 500 milliseconds or a rise above 60 milliseconds from baseline is the action threshold
Replace magnesium even when only mildly low because it stabilises the myocardium
Citalopram prolongs the interval in a dose dependent way with a specific maximum dose warning
Correct the reversible physiology first, then rationalise the psychotropic regimen
explanation.pearls: Replace potassium to the upper half of the reference range rather than merely into it when the corrected QT exceeds 500 milliseconds, and give magnesium regardless of a borderline level, because serum magnesium correlates poorly with total body stores.

subtopic_detail: involuntary movements and a suggestive family history in apparent treatment resistant depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 41 year old man referred with eighteen months of low mood, irritability and loss of interest that has not responded to adequate trials of two antidepressants. He works as an accountant and has been placed on a performance review at work.

His wife says the bigger change is that he has become blunt to the point of rudeness with her family, has spent several thousand dollars on impulse purchases, and no longer initiates anything at home. She also mentions that he fidgets constantly, drops cups and cutlery, and that his walking has become unsteady in a way he does not seem to notice. He has never been prescribed an antipsychotic or any dopamine blocking medication. His mother died at 55 in a psychiatric hospital with what the family were told was early dementia.

data_table.Examination: Brief irregular involuntary movements of the fingers and face incorporated into voluntary gestures, motor impersistence with inability to maintain tongue protrusion for ten seconds, slowed initiation of horizontal saccades, wide based unsteady gait, no cogwheel rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function within normal limits, vitamin B12 within normal limits, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology negative, full blood count within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial a third antidepressant from a different class for three months
options.rationale: Two adequate trials have failed and the presentation includes a progressive movement disorder and executive change that no antidepressant explains. Further sequential trials are the mechanism by which this diagnosis is typically delayed for years. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Send the huntingtin gene test from the clinic today and phone the result
options.rationale: The test itself is the right test, which is what makes this tempting, but delivering a result of this kind without pre test counselling, assessment of the patient's understanding, and planning for how at risk relatives will be informed is contrary to established practice. Each of his children carries a one in two prior risk and their position must be considered before the result exists. (Source: Human Genetics Society of Australasia)

options.text: Refer to a neurogenetics service for counselling before any genetic test
options.rationale: Progressive personality change with apathy and disinhibition, chorea with motor impersistence and slowed saccades, and a parent who died young with a psychiatric and cognitive illness together indicate an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder. Testing for it carries profound implications for the patient, his children and his insurance and employment, so it is performed within a genetic counselling framework rather than ordered from a psychiatric clinic. (Source: Human Genetics Society of Australasia)

options.text: Commence an antipsychotic to suppress the involuntary movements now
options.rationale: Dopamine blocking agents including tetrabenazine are used for functionally disabling chorea later in the illness, so this is a treatment on the right pathway at the wrong time. Starting one before the diagnosis is established obscures the movement disorder and risks it being reattributed to the drug. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and review the report
options.rationale: Imaging may show caudate atrophy with enlarged frontal horns but this appears relatively late and a normal scan would not exclude the diagnosis. It is a supportive investigation rather than the step that resolves the question. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

explanation.summary: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene, with full penetrance at 40 or more repeats and anticipation through paternal transmission. Psychiatric and behavioural change frequently precedes the movement disorder by years, and irritability, apathy, disinhibition and depression are the usual presentations, which is why these patients often reach a psychiatric service first and accumulate several failed antidepressant trials. The motor signs to seek deliberately are chorea, often absorbed into apparently purposeful gestures early on, motor impersistence demonstrated by inability to sustain tongue protrusion or a steady grip, and slowed or delayed initiation of saccades, which is one of the earliest reliable findings. A family history may be obscured, since a parent who died young of another cause, or whose illness was labelled as early dementia, alcoholism or a psychiatric disorder, is common. Testing is performed through a genetic service because the result determines risk for children and siblings who have not asked to know, and because suicide risk around the time of diagnosis is elevated.
key_points: Psychiatric and behavioural change often precedes chorea by several years
Motor impersistence and slowed saccades are early and easily missed signs
Chorea is initially incorporated into voluntary movements and looks like fidgeting
A parent labelled with early dementia or alcoholism may represent an obscured family history
Genetic testing proceeds through a counselling framework because relatives are implicated
explanation.pearls: Ask the patient to protrude the tongue and hold it out for ten seconds, and to grip your fingers steadily: inability to sustain either, known as motor impersistence, appears early in Huntington disease and is often present before chorea is obvious enough to be noticed by the family.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists
